data.name: Warm and dense matter
data.description: Warm dense matter can refer to either equilibrium or non-equilibrium states of matter in a (loosely defined) regime of temperature and density between condensed matter and hot plasma. It can be defined as the state that is too dense to be described by weakly coupled plasma physics yet too hot to be described by condensed matter physics. In this state, the potential energy of the interaction between electrons and nuclei and the kinetic energy of electrons are of roughly the same magnitude. The temperature is of the order of the Fermi energy. A commonly occurring type of WDM, created using ultra-fast laser pulses, may exist for a short time in a two-temperature quasi-equilibrium form where the electrons are very hot and have a temperature different from the ions. WDM has a density of the same order of magnitude as a solid (typically somewhere between 0.01 and 100 grams per cc) and a temperature on the order of several thousand kelvins (typically somewhere between 0.5 and 100 electronvolts/Boltzmann constant, in the units favored by practitioners). In effect, WDM is a sub-category of warm-correlated matter.  WDM is expected in the cores of giant planets, brown dwarfs, and small stars. WDM is also created in the inertial confinement fusion context during the solid to plasma phase transition driven by laser pulses, and other systems that start as solids and are heated to become strongly interacting plasmas. The latter two categories imply that WDM physics are also relevant not only to nuclear explosions, but also to atmospheric entry from space, ablation of metals, laser-machining of materials etc. In effect, warm dense matter is also created during intense laser-target interactions[2] and particle beam-target interactions.

data.name: Multiphoton Ionisation
data.description: Photoionization is the physical process in which an ion is formed from the interaction of a photon with an atom or molecule. For photon energies below the ionization threshold, the photoionization cross-section is near zero. But with the development of pulsed lasers it has become possible to create extremely intense, coherent light where multi-photon ionization may occur. At even higher intensities, non-perturbative phenomena such as barrier suppression ionization and rescattering ionization are observed.

data.name: Cyberpsychology
data.description: Cyberpsychology is a field of psychology that focuses on the study of human behavior and the psychological processes related to the use of technology and the internet. This includes examining how people interact with technology, how they perceive and process information online, and how online behavior and activities impact their psychological well-being. Cyberpsychology also explores the impact of technology and the internet on social and cultural dynamics, as well as ethical considerations related to the use of technology in various contexts. In essence, cyberpsychology seeks to understand the complex interplay between technology and the human mind and behavior.

It includes processes common to all management like planning, organizing, staffing, directing and controlling. It is common for registered nurses to seek additional education to earn a Master of Science in Nursing or Doctor of Nursing Practice to prepare for leadership roles within nursing. data.name: European Economics
data.description: The economy of Europe comprises about 748 million people in 50 countries. The formation of the European Union (EU) and in 1999 the introduction of a unified currency, the Euro, brought participating European countries closer through the convenience of a shared currency and has led to a stronger European cash flow. The European Union is a unique global organisation, an entity forming one of the largest economies in the world. The European Union also “regulates” the global market by the single market.

The study of photochemical systems that use sunlight to drive important chemical reactions or to generate electricity is of great practical significance for the development of sustainable sources of energy.

data.name: Blockchain
data.description: A blockchain is a dynamic list of records called blocks that are linked over time. Each block contains a cryptographic hash of the previous block, a timestamp and transaction data. By design, a blockchain is resistant to modification of its data. The concept of a blockchain was invented to serve as the public transaction ledger of the cryptocurrency Bitcoin. For use as a distributed ledger, a blockchain is typically managed by a peer-to-peer network collectively adhering to a protocol for inter-node communication and for validating new blocks. Although blockchain records are not unalterable, blockchains may be considered secure by design and exemplify a distributed computing system with high Byzantine fault tolerance. Associated concepts include: Ethereum, smart contracts, Byzantine protocol, decentralized control.

data.name: Nuclear Energy

data.name: Electrical Machines
data.description: In electrical engineering, electric machine is a general term for machines using electromagnetic forces, such as electric motors, electric generators, and others. They are electromechanical energy converters: an electric motor converts electricity to mechanical power while an electric generator converts mechanical power to electricity. The moving parts in a machine can be rotating (rotating machines) or linear (linear machines). Besides motors and generators, a third category often included is transformers, which although they do not have any moving parts are also energy converters, changing the voltage level of an alternating current

data.name: Learning and Memory

Learning refers to the process of acquiring new knowledge or skills through experience, instruction, or observation, while memory is the ability to store and retrieve information over time. Together, they play a crucial role in cognitive functioning, skill development, and adaptive behavior.

data.name: Social Influence
data.description: Social influence, in the field of psychology, refers to the process through which individuals' thoughts, feelings, and behaviors are influenced by the presence, actions, or opinions of others. It examines how social factors and group dynamics shape individuals' attitudes, beliefs, and actions, leading to conformity, compliance, or obedience.

data.name: Intelligence Development
data.description: Intelligence development, in the field of psychology, refers to the process through which an individual's cognitive abilities and intellectual functioning evolve and mature over time. It encompasses the acquisition, enhancement, and utilization of cognitive skills, including reasoning, problem-solving, memory, attention, language, and learning. Intelligence development is influenced by a complex interplay of genetic, biological, environmental, and socio-cultural factors. It is not a fixed trait but rather a dynamic and malleable construct that can be shaped and influenced through various experiences, education, and environmental stimuli. Intelligence development is often studied through the examination of individual differences, developmental trajectories, and changes in cognitive abilities across the lifespan.

subjects.term: Intelligence. Mental ability. Intelligence testing. Ability testing

data.name: Organizational Psychology
data.description: Organizational psychology, also known as industrial-organizational (I-O) psychology, is a field of study within psychology that focuses on understanding and improving human behavior in the workplace. It applies psychological theories, principles, and research methods to enhance individual and organizational effectiveness, well-being, and productivity.

data.name: Aggression
data.description: Aggression, in the field of psychology, refers to behavior that is intended to cause harm or infliction of physical or psychological pain on others. It involves acts such as physical violence, verbal aggression, and hostile behavior. Aggression can be influenced by various factors, including individual differences, social and cultural factors, and situational triggers.

data.name: Prosocial Behavior
data.description: Prosocial behavior in the field of psychology refers to voluntary actions intended to benefit others or promote the well-being of individuals or society as a whole. It involves acts of kindness, empathy, cooperation, and altruism that contribute to positive social interactions and the betterment of communities.

data.name: Instructional Psychology
data.description: Instructional psychology is a field of study that focuses on understanding and optimizing the processes of teaching and learning. It involves the application of psychological principles, theories, and research to enhance instructional practices and improve educational outcomes. Instructional theorists and psychologists aim to develop and refine instructional models and approaches based on empirical evidence and psychological principles to facilitate effective teaching and maximize students' acquisition of knowledge and skills.

data.name: Cognition
data.description: Cognition in the field of psychology refers to the mental processes and abilities involved in acquiring, processing, storing, and using information. It encompasses various aspects of thinking, including perception, attention, memory, language, problem-solving, and decision-making.

data.name: Developmental Disabilities
data.description: Developmental disabilities, in the field of psychology, refer to a group of conditions that manifest early in life and result in significant limitations in an individual's cognitive, social, emotional, and physical development. These disabilities are typically chronic and lifelong, and they can affect various aspects of functioning, including intellectual abilities, language and communication skills, motor coordination, and adaptive behavior. Developmental disabilities can arise due to a combination of genetic, environmental, and neurodevelopmental factors.

subjects.term: Intellectual disabilities; developmental and learning disorders

data.name: Clinical Social Work
data.description: Clinical social work is a specialized field within social work that focuses on the assessment, diagnosis, and treatment of individuals, families, and communities who are experiencing various mental health and psychosocial issues. Clinical social workers are trained professionals who provide therapeutic interventions, counseling, and support to clients in order to enhance their overall well-being and functioning. They work in diverse settings such as hospitals, clinics, schools, and private practices, collaborating with other professionals to address clients' emotional, behavioral, and social needs. The field of clinical social work integrates principles from social work, psychology, and psychiatry to provide comprehensive and holistic care to individuals and communities.

subjects.term: People with mental illness and disabilities

data.name: Mental Disorder
data.description: In the field of psychology, mental disorder refers to a broad range of conditions characterized by significant disturbances in thoughts, emotions, behaviors, and functioning. Mental disorders are studied within the context of understanding their causes, symptoms, diagnosis, treatment, and prevention. Researchers and clinicians in the field of mental disorders aim to classify and understand these conditions, explore their impact on individuals' well-being and daily functioning, and develop effective interventions and support systems.

data.name: Cancer Epidemiology
data.description: Cancer epidemiology is the study of the distribution, determinants, and frequency of cancer in populations

subjects.term: Incidence of and public measures to prevent disease

data.name: Sensory Psychology
data.description: Sensory Psychology refers to the study of sensation, which is the process by which our sensory receptors, such as the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, and skin, detect and respond to external stimuli.

data.name: Behaviorial Therapy
data.description: Behavioral therapy, also known as behavior therapy, is an approach within the field of psychology that focuses on modifying and changing problematic behaviors by utilizing principles of learning theory. It is rooted in the belief that behaviors are learned and can be unlearned or replaced with more adaptive behaviors through systematic interventions. Behavioral therapy emphasizes the role of the environment in shaping behavior and utilizes techniques such as positive reinforcement, negative reinforcement, and behavior modification to promote positive change.

data.name: Person-Centered Psychotherapy
data.description: Person-Centered Psychotherapy, also known as Client-Centered Therapy or Rogerian Therapy, is a humanistic approach to psychotherapy developed by Carl Rogers. It emphasizes the importance of the therapeutic relationship and provides a supportive and non-judgmental environment for individuals to explore their feelings, experiences, and self-perceptions. The therapist adopts an empathic and unconditional positive regard towards the client, allowing them to gain self-awareness, self-acceptance, and personal growth.

data.name: Self-Regulation
data.description: Self-regulation is a field of study in psychology that focuses on the processes and strategies individuals use to manage and control their thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. It encompasses the ability to set goals, monitor one's progress, and make adjustments in order to achieve desired outcomes. Self-regulation involves a range of cognitive, emotional, and behavioral processes, such as attention control, impulse control, emotion regulation, self-monitoring, and self-reflection.

data.name: Advertising Psychology
data.description: Advertising psychology is a subfield within the broader discipline of consumer behavior that focuses specifically on the psychological processes involved in advertising and marketing. It seeks to understand how consumers perceive, process, and respond to advertising messages, as well as how advertisers can use this information to create more effective and persuasive campaigns.

data.name: Customer Satisfaction
data.description: Customer satisfaction refers to the overall evaluation or assessment that customers make of a product or service they have used or purchased. It is an important construct in the field of consumer behavior, which seeks to understand how consumers think, feel, and behave in relation to different products and services. Customer satisfaction is typically measured through a variety of metrics, including survey-based measures, customer feedback, and online reviews. The goal of measuring customer satisfaction is to identify areas of strengths and weaknesses in a product or service and to use this information to improve customer experiences and build brand loyalty. In addition, customer satisfaction is a key predictor of future consumer behavior, including repeat purchases, recommendations to others, and overall brand engagement.

data.name: Internet Psychology
data.description: Internet psychology is a field of study that focuses on the psychological aspects of online behavior and interactions, including social, cognitive, and emotional processes that occur in digital environments. It examines the ways in which people use the internet, how they perceive and experience online interactions, and the impact of technology on psychological processes and outcomes. Internet psychology draws on various disciplines such as psychology, computer science, sociology, and communication studies to understand topics such as online identity, cyberbullying, social media addiction, online privacy, online learning, and virtual communities. The field aims to inform the design and use of digital technologies, as well as to improve individuals' well-being and quality of life in the online world.

data.name: Psychological Testing
data.description: Psychological testing refers to the use of standardized and objective methods to measure various aspects of an individual's psychological functioning, including personality traits, cognitive abilities, and emotional states. These tests are designed to provide reliable and valid information about an individual's psychological characteristics, and they are typically administered and interpreted by trained professionals, such as psychologists or psychometricians. Psychological testing can be used in a variety of settings, including clinical assessment, educational and vocational planning, and research.

data.name: Qualitative Psychology
data.description: Qualitative psychology is an approach within the field of psychology that focuses on understanding and exploring the subjective experiences, meanings, and interpretations of individuals. It emphasizes the use of qualitative research methods to gain in-depth insights into the complexities of human behavior, thoughts, and emotions. Unlike quantitative psychology, which relies on numerical data and statistical analyses, qualitative psychology emphasizes the collection and analysis of non-numerical data, such as interviews, observations, and textual materials.

data.name: Stereotype
data.description: Stereotype, in the field of psychology, refers to a widely held belief or generalization about a particular group or category of people. Stereotypes are cognitive shortcuts that allow individuals to quickly categorize and make assumptions about others based on their group membership. They can be positive, negative, or neutral and often involve oversimplified and exaggerated characteristics or attributes.

data.name: Twentieth-Century Literature
data.description: Literary works written in the twentieth century, from 1900 to 1999. Includes major literary movements such as modernism and postmodernism, as well as Edwardian literature and writing of the First World War, Second World War and Cold War.

data.name: Policy Formulation
data.description: It is the process of arriving at statements by organizing policy resources and supporting information to convert ideas into solutions that are practically implementable to deal with certain activity or address challenges evolved therewith and which are in the direction of the policy objectives.

data.name: Agenda Setting
data.description: The political process in which policies and policy issues are prioritized and considered for action by governments. It can be influenced by numerous factors, including the public, the media, policymakers and interest groups.

data.name: Policy Adoption
data.description: The stage in the policy-making process in which a policy or course of action is agreed upon in order to achieve a particular policy goal. Policy adoption is a part of the decision to choose policy alternatives after the policy formulation process. Mostly, the policy adoption process is influenced by internal and external determinants, often called policy diffusion. These determinants are each associated with elements that influence a government's decision to adopt a policy.

data.name: Policy Implementation
data.description: Implementation of policy by state and non-state actors on a global, regional and municipal scale. Policy implementation literature typically distinguishes between top-down and bottom-up approaches. The public sector generally, and national governments in particular, no longer detain a monopoly on policy implementation. Different agencies and levels of government can be involved in the implementation of policies and initiatives, representing diverse and often conflicting interests. Indeed in many cases, policies are not implemented by those who design it, and sometimes they are pursued by actors or stakeholders from outside the public administration.  Successful policy implementation is largely dependent on the government and other actors having the right tools at hand to identify the nature and dimensions of those challenges and to formulate and design adequate policy responses to address them.

data.name: Policy Evaluation
data.description: Policy evaluation examines the content, implementation, merit, worth and impact of policies.

data.name: Comparative Public Policy
data.description: An area of study that analyses and compares public policy across different systems, institutions, countries or governments.

data.name: Migration Policy
data.description: The study of government policies, statements, decisions, orders, and/or laws and regulations, regarding the selections, admission, settlement and deportation of foreign citizens residing in the country.

data.name: Energy System Transformation
data.description: The study of the policies concerning the shift from non-renewable to renewable energy sources. This often includes studying the governance and adoption of new technologies.

Energy industries. Energy policy. Fuel trade

data.name: Urban Policy
data.description: The study of policies aimed at influencing the development of towns and cities, as well as their inhabitants.

Urban groups. The city. Urban sociology
Regional, state and other local government

data.name: Public Management
data.description: Public management is an area of political science that studies the way government programmes are managed

data.name: Governance and Government
data.description: Government refers to the offices, departments and groups of people who control a political unit. Governance refers to the systems and processes by which those people act, operate and make policies and decisions.

data.name: Methodology of Political Science
data.description: The methods and ways in which political science is studied. This can be both quantitative and qualitative, including statistics and discourse research.

subjects.term: Theory. Method. Scope. Relations to other subjects

data.name: Political Education
data.description: Political Education involves the teaching and learning of political knowledge, skills, and values, aiming to develop informed and engaged citizens capable of participating in democratic processes.

data.name: American Politics
data.description: American Politics studies the political system of the United States, including its institutions, processes, behavior, and policies, as well as the historical and contemporary issues shaping American governance.

subjects.term: Political institutions and public administration (United States)
Political institutions and public administration (Canada, Latin America, etc.)

data.name: Childhood Education
data.description: Early Childhood Care and Education (ECCE) in the Indian context is generally defined as the care and education of children from birth to eight years. It includes: Early stimulation programmes through crèches/homes stimulation for 0-3 year olds.  Education is the foundation of a child's future well-being. Children's education creates various opportunities to help them live better lives. It can also help shape the society at large. With the right education, a child can help the country develop and progress at a faster pace.

data.name: Social Work Consulting
data.description: Social work consulting is a field of study that focuses on providing expert guidance, advice, and support to individuals, organizations, and communities in addressing social issues and improving social work practices. Social work consultants apply their knowledge, skills, and experience to offer specialized insights, recommendations, and solutions to enhance the effectiveness and impact of social work interventions and programs.

subjects.term: Social service. Social work. Charity organization and practice

data.name: Theory and Method in Social Work
data.description: Theory and method in social work refer to the foundational frameworks, concepts, and approaches used to understand and address social issues, as well as the systematic procedures and techniques employed in social work practice. Theories provide the theoretical underpinnings and conceptual frameworks that inform social work interventions, while methods outline the systematic steps and techniques used to implement these interventions and achieve desired outcomes.

synonyms: Theorie und Methode in der Sozialen Arbeit

subjects.term: Social service. Social work. Charity organization and practice

data.name: Social Care
data.description: Social care is the provision of services and support to individuals and families to aid their physical, emotional, and social well-being, including child protection, elder care, and assistance for people with disabilities or mental health issues.

data.name: Sports Communication
data.description: Sports communication is an area of study that seeks to understand the relationship between communication processes and sport contexts. Communication processes refer to the creation and understanding of meaning through exchanging verbal and nonverbal messages. It can encompass the study of interpersonal and organizational communication between players, coaches, managers, referees, trainers and physiotherapists, and governing bodies, as well as communication between sports participants, fans, and the media and way in which sports are represented and communicated in the media. the methods used to study Sports Communication range from quantitative over qualitative approaches up to frameworks in critical and cultural studies. Studies in sports communication have addressed subjects such as audience reactions to mediated sporting contests; communication between coaches and athletes; media portrayals of athletes based on considerations such as gender, race, and nationality; and the professional routines of sports media practitioners.

subjects.term: Athletic and outdoor sports and games

data.name: Sport Theory
data.description: Sport Theory encompasses theoretical knowledge and analysis in the fields of biology, training theory, kinematics, as well as psychological, social and sociopolitical aspects of sport. In this regard, Sport theory draws on concepts from political sciences and sociological theories (such as theories of conflict and exchange, funcionalist, interactionalist, critical and feminist or figurational theories),  as well on concepts from philosophy end ethics to understand and explain the significance of sport in a more fundamental way.

data.name: Sport Analytics
data.description: Sport Analytics refers to the use of data and statistical methods to measure and evaluate performance for the purpose of being able to make decisions to improve performance and gain advantage over competing teams or athletes. Sport analytics is used during and prior to sport events and can inform players, coaches and other parties in aspects of game tactics, player fitness and health as well as the business of a sports organisation.

subjects.term: Athletic and outdoor sports and games

data.name: Sport Technology
data.description: Sport Technology is a area of study connecting sport science and engineering. Some subfields of Sport Technology are equipment and clothic technology, sports informatics, Sports measurement technology or Performance Diagnostics. Sport Technology might refer to any of the different uses of technical resources and devices in a sport context. Technology is applied to assist athletes, rehabilitate after injuries and increase performance, either during sport activities in the form of specialized gear or in preparation, evaluation and training (e.g. self monitoring, data bases, data evaluation). Technology is also applied for monitoring, broadcasting and to assist referees (usually in the form of computer software and cameras), as well as to manipulate the sporting environment (arena architecture, sport tracks/fields etc.)  Technology affects many aspects of sport from performance on and off the field to spectating and public profile. The use of technology in Sport is therefore ambivalent and might have positive and negative impact on sport from the perspective of athletes, officials or spectators

data.name: Sport Psychology
data.description: Sport Psychologyis is concerned with the preconditions and determining factors of the behaviour and experience of individuals (persons) in sport.  It aims at the adequate unterstanding of the behaviour and the experience of individuals in sport by describing and measuring consistency and variability, by offering explanations, as well as by determining their preconditions and possibilities to predict and shape its future course.  More specifically, Sport Psychology explores the processes of perception and decision making during sports games, the emergence or reduction of emotions (such as fear), the determining factors of an active lifestyle, the impact of sport on the development of children or the personality and group features of successful athletes and teams.

data.name: Sport History
data.description: Sport History aims at analyzing the sporting past by following socially relevant questions with the help of methodic instruments of historical science. It is concerned with historical events related to sports, the development of contemporary sport and its various cultural origins and predecessors, as well as with the shifting meaning of sport for individuals and social groups across time.

data.name: Sport Training
data.description: Sport Training refers to the special process of preparation of athletes and sports persons based on scientific principles aimed at improving and maintaining higher performance capacity in different sports activities. Training is designed to improve overall fitness and the abilities necessary to perform in a given sport, which might include strength training, practice of movement patterns, corrective and restorative exercises, conditioning and cardiovascular training, mental and psychological training and advise on nutrition. Sport training is usually an individual-specific process aided by scientific methods and findings and supported by a coaching person. It therefore involves some degree of education of the athlete and not only aims at improvement of physical fitness, but also at the acquisition of specific sports skills, improvement of tactical efficiency and mental abilities.

data.name: Redox Biology
data.description: Redox biology is a branch of biology that focuses on the role of redox (oxidation-reduction) reactions in various biological processes. It explores the interplay between reactive oxygen species (ROS) and antioxidants in living organisms.

subjects.term: General biochemistry of plants and animals

data.name: Cell Differentiation
data.description: Cell differentiation is the process by which specialised cells such as muscle, skin or nerve cells, are formed from less specialised cells. Differentiation occurs during development of an organism to produce new specialised cells, and also in adults to replenish cells that are lost.

data.name: Embryology
data.description: Embryology is the discipline concerned with the study of embryogenesis, the development of the embryo from a fertilised egg cell. Findings in embryology have helped in the understanding of congenital abnormalities and developing assisted reproduction procedures.

data.name: Behavioral Ecology
data.description: Behavioural ecology is the study of behavioural interactions between individuals within populations and communities, usually in an evolutionary context. It looks at how competition and cooperation between and within species affects evolutionary fitness.

data.name: Evolutionary Developmental Biology
data.description: Evolutionary developmental biology is the comparative study of organismal development and how it has evolved. There is a particular focus on the genetic basis of phenotypic structures, how they change during evolution, and how novel structures arise.

data.name: Sound Studies
data.description: Sound Studies is an interdisciplinary field exploring the cultural, historical, and technological dimensions of sound and listening. It examines how practices like voice, noise, silence, and aural perception are shaped by society and media, with an emphasis on sound reproduction technologies.

data.name: International and Intercultural Communication
data.description: Intercultural communication refers to how communication behavior is affected when people from different cultures interact and differ in how they perceive the world around them. One way to understand intercultural communication is to see it as communication that unfolds in symbolic intercultural spaces.

data.name: Media and Communication Methods
data.description: A field covering research methods and techniques, including research design, the collection, analysis and interpretation of data in media and communication studies.

synonyms: Methoden der Kommunikationsforschung: Methoden der Medienforschung

data.name: Media and Gender
data.description: Media and gender refers to the relationship between mass media and gender, and how gender is represented within media platforms.

data.name: Media Reception and Media Effects
data.description: Media influence and media effects are topics relating to mass media and media culture's effects on individual or an audience's thoughts, attitudes, and behavior. Whether it is written, televised, or spoken, mass media reaches a large audience. Mass media's role and effect in shaping modern culture are central issues for study of culture.

data.name: Media and Globalisation
data.description: The process of the production, distribution, and consumption of media products on a global scale, facilitating the exchange and diffusion of ideas cross-culturally.

data.name: Social Media
data.description: Forms of electronic communication (such as websites for social networking and microblogging) through which users create online communities to share information, ideas, personal messages, and other content.  Social Media studies explores the relationship to and impact of this form of communication on culture, society, psychology, politics etc.

subjects.term: Media studies: internet, digital media and society

data.name: Advertising
data.description: The activity or profession of producing advertisements for commercial products or services.

data.name: Public Relations
data.description: Public relations (PR) is the practice of managing and disseminating information from an individual or an organization (such as a business, government agency, or a nonprofit organization) to the public in order to affect their public perception. Public relations (PR) and publicity differ in that PR is controlled internally, whereas publicity is not controlled and contributed by external parties.

data.name: Sociological Methods
data.description: Sociological methods refer to the techniques and approaches used by sociologists to collect, analyze, and interpret data in order to study social phenomena. These methods enable researchers to investigate and understand various aspects of society, such as social structures, institutions, behaviors, and processes.

data.name: Biographical Research
data.description: Biographical research is a qualitative research approach aligned to the social interpretive paradigm of research. The biographical research is concerned with the reconstruction of life histories and the constitution of meaning based on biographical narratives and documents.

data.name: Sociology of Food and Nutrition
data.description: The sociology of food and nutrition, or food sociology, concentrates on the myriad sociocultural, political, economic and philosophical factors that influence our food habits— what we eat, when we eat, how we eat and why we eat.

subjects.term: Theory. Method. Relations to other subjects

data.name: Network Research
data.description: Network Research involves the study of networks, including social, biological, and technological networks, focusing on their structure, dynamics, and impact on various phenomena.

data.name: Public Sociology
data.description: Public Sociology is a subfield of sociology that focuses on the engagement of sociological knowledge and methods with the public, aiming to address societal issues, promote public discourse, and empower social change. This includes collaboration with non-academic audiences, such as policymakers, activists, and communities.

synonyms: Sociological knowledge and methods with the public

data.name: Immune Cell Signalling
data.description: Immune cell signaling refers to the communication processes that occur between different immune cells in the immune system. These signaling events play a crucial role in coordinating and regulating the immune response to various pathogens, foreign substances, and abnormal cells. Immune cell signaling ensures effective immune surveillance, activation, and coordination of immune cell activities.

data.name: Lymphatic System
data.description: The lymphatic system is a network of lymphoid organs and lymphatic vessels. It transports lymph fluid and helps to clear toxins and other waste from the body’s tissues. Lymphocytes use the lymphatic system to circulate throughout the body, but it can also facilitate the spread of cancer cells.

subjects.term: SCIENCE / Life Sciences / Anatomy & Physiology (see also Life Sciences / Human Anatomy & Physiology)

data.name: Biofilms
data.description: Biofilms are communities of microorganisms that attach to each other and to surfaces, for example by bacterial adherence. Biofilms consist of both the cells and the extracellular matrix produced by the cells. Biofilms can be problematic in certain places, for example inside pipes or on medical implants.

subjects.term: Ecology, organisms characteristic of specific environments

data.name: DNA Damage and Repair
data.description: DNA damage and repair refers to the creation and correction of DNA lesions that threaten genome integrity. Because DNA replication errors or environmental agents that damage DNA can introduce mutations if not corrected, multiple cellular DNA repair mechanisms exist to remove damaged regions of chromosomes to prevent these potentially deleterious effects.

data.name: Bone Physiology
data.description: Bone physiology involves the coordinated regulation of a myriad of biological processes that lead tissue development, homeostasis and repair upon trauma.

subjects.term: SCIENCE / Life Sciences / Anatomy & Physiology (see also Life Sciences / Human Anatomy & Physiology)

data.name: Renal Physiology
data.description: This encompasses all functions of the kidney, including maintenance of acid-base balance; regulation of fluid balance; regulation of sodium, potassium, and other electrolytes; clearance of toxins; absorption of glucose, amino acids, and other small molecules; regulation of blood pressure; production of various hormones, such as erythropoietin; and activation of vitamin D.

subjects.term: SCIENCE / Life Sciences / Anatomy & Physiology (see also Life Sciences / Human Anatomy & Physiology)

data.name: Hepatic Physiology
data.description: The liver plays a role in nearly every organ system in the body. It interacts with the endocrine and gastrointestinal systems by aiding in digestion and metabolism. The liver is the storage location for fat-soluble vitamins and handles cholesterol homeostasis. It stores iron and copper.

subjects.term: SCIENCE / Life Sciences / Anatomy & Physiology (see also Life Sciences / Human Anatomy & Physiology)

data.name: Muscle Physiology
data.description: Muscle physiology is the branch of physiology that studies the function, mechanisms, and regulation of muscle tissue. It includes the processes underlying muscle contraction, such as the interaction of actin and myosin and the roles of calcium ions and ATP, as well as the neuromuscular junction, where motor neurons transmit signals to muscle fibers. Muscle physiology also encompasses different muscle types (skeletal, cardiac, and smooth) and examines how muscles respond and adapt to stimuli such as exercise, injury, and disease.

subjects.term: SCIENCE / Life Sciences / Anatomy & Physiology (see also Life Sciences / Human Anatomy & Physiology)

data.name: Digestive System Physiology
data.description: The function of the digestive system is to digest and absorb food and then excrete the waste products with the help of the liver, gallbladder, pancreas, small intestine, large intestine, and rectum. Each of these organs plays a specific role in the digestive system.

subjects.term: SCIENCE / Life Sciences / Anatomy & Physiology (see also Life Sciences / Human Anatomy & Physiology)
Physiology of the digestive tract. Digestion

data.name: International Political Economy
data.description: International Political Economy examines the interplay between politics and economics on a global scale, analyzing how political institutions, economic systems, and international relations shape global economic outcomes.

subjects.term: POLITICAL SCIENCE / International Relations / Trade & Tariffs

data.name: Educational Research
data.description: Educational research refers to the systematic study and investigation of educational topics, issues, and phenomena. It is a field of inquiry that aims to generate new knowledge, advance understanding, and improve educational practices and policies. Educational research encompasses a wide range of methodologies, approaches, and areas of study, addressing various aspects of teaching, learning, curriculum, assessment, and educational systems.

data.name: Sport Education and Didactics
data.description: Sport Education is a curriculum and instruction model designed for delivery within physical education. Modifications can be made to suit each age category, activity or setting. It is most effective with games based activities and with participants who have a good base level of competence. Didactics refers to the science of teaching and instruction for any given field of study. Based on theoretical foundations, a didactic approach involves a very structured and informed approach to teaching and instruction.

data.name: Adult Education
data.description: Adult education is education aimed at mature students that have already taken part in the workforce. Learning as a mature student gives individuals the chance to gain new skills and expand their knowledge.

subjects.term: Education extension. Adult education. Continuing education

data.name: Analytical Aesthetics
data.description: A branch of philosophy that deals with the nature of beauty and taste, as well as the philosophy of art.

data.name: Media Ethics
data.description: Media ethics is a division of applied ethics dealing with the specific ethical principles and standards of media, including broadcast media, film, theatre, the arts, print media and the internet.

data.name: Philosophy of the 17th century
data.description: The philosophy of the 17th century was a significant period of intellectual development that witnessed the emergence of groundbreaking philosophical ideas and debates. some key aspects and figures associated with the philosophy of the 17th century Rationalism, Empiricism, Dualism.

subjects.term: Philosophical traditions and schools of thought

data.name: Philosophy of the 18th century
data.description: The philosophy of the 18th century, also known as the Enlightenment, was a period of significant intellectual and philosophical development in Europe. It was marked by a strong emphasis on reason, science, and progress, as well as criticism of traditional authority and superstition. some key aspects and figures associated with the philosophy of the 18th century Rationalism and Empiricism, Social Contract Theory, Natural Rights and Individualism, Skepticism and Criticism, Utilitarianism
