data.name: Philosophy of the 19th century
data.description: Philosophy from the late 1700s through the very early 1900s is considered philosophy of the "long 19th century." In Western philosophy, 19th century philosophy tends to begin with Kant and end with Freud and Du Bois as thinkers bridging 19th and 20th centuries.

subjects.term: Philosophical traditions and schools of thought

data.name: Philosophy of the 20th century
data.description: The philosophy of the 20th century witnessed a diverse range of philosophical movements and ideas, reflecting the intellectual and cultural developments of the time. Some key aspects and figures associated with the philosophy of the 20th century Analytic Philosophy, Phenomenology, Existentialism, Pragmatism, Continental Philosophy, Post-structuralism and Deconstruction, Analytical Marxism and Critical Theory.

subjects.term: Philosophical traditions and schools of thought

data.name: Buddhist philosophy
data.description: Buddhist philosophy is the ancient Indian philosophical system that developed within the religio-philosophical tradition of Buddhism.[2] It comprises all the philosophical investigations and systems of rational inquiry that developed among various schools of Buddhism in ancient India following the parinirvāṇa of Gautama Buddha (c. 5th century BCE), as well as the further developments which followed the spread of Buddhism throughout Asia.

data.name: Postcolonial Philosophy
data.description: Postcolonial Philosophy arose in the 20th century as a methodology and tradition for thinking critically about the afterlives of colonialism and its ongoing impacts on the Global South.

subjects.term: Modern western and other noneastern philosophy
Philosophical traditions and schools of thought

data.name: Philosophy of Feelings
data.description: The Philosophy of Feelings is a branch of philosophy that examines the nature and role of human feelings, including emotions, affective states, and subjective experiences. It investigates questions concerning the origin, ontology, phenomenology, and ethical implications of feelings.

data.name: Mind-Body Problem/Body-Soul Problem
data.description: The mind–body problem is a debate concerning the relationship between thought and consciousness in the human mind, and the brain as part of the physical body.

data.name: Pragmatism
data.description: Pragmatisim is a tradition rooted in 19th and early 20th century American philosophy and is characterized by its theorization from lived experience.

data.name: Neo-Kantianism
data.description: Neo-Kantianism refers to a philosophical movement that emerged in the late 19th and early 20th centuries as a reinterpretation and development of Immanuel Kant's ideas. It sought to update Kant's philosophy in light of new developments in science, logic, and philosophy itself.

data.name: Materialism
data.description: Materialism is a philosophical perspective that posits that the physical or material world is the fundamental reality, and that all phenomena, including mental states and consciousness, can ultimately be explained in terms of material or physical processes. Materialists assert that everything, including thoughts, emotions, and consciousness, can be reduced to and explained by the interactions of matter and physical forces.

data.name: Empiricism
data.description: Empiricism is the thesis that knowledge is derived from experience. Empiricism is a philosophical approach that emphasizes the importance of sensory experience and empirical evidence as the foundation for acquiring knowledge and understanding the world. It holds that knowledge originates primarily from observation, experimentation, and direct sensory experience, rather than relying on innate ideas or theoretical speculation. Empiricists believe that knowledge can be gained through the senses, and they often seek to validate or refute hypotheses through observable evidence and data.

subjects.term: Philosophy: epistemology and theory of knowledge

data.name: Speech Act Theory
data.description: Speech act theory is a branch of pragmatics and the philosophy of language that explores how utterances function not only to convey information but also to perform actions. It investigates the communicative acts performed by speakers through their use of language and the ways in which language is used to accomplish various actions.

subjects.term: Psychological principles, language acquisition, speech perception

data.name: Analytical Philosophy of Language
data.description: Analytical philosophy of language is a specific subfield within the philosophy of language that focuses on the philosophical analysis of language using logical and analytical methods. It emerged primarily in the 20th century and is associated with the tradition of analytic philosophy.

data.name: Continental Philosophy
data.description: Continental Philosophy refers to non-Anglophone European philosophy of the 20th and 21st centuries (primarily phenomenology, existentialism, poststructuralism, postmodernism, deconstruction, critical theory, and Marxism) and Anglophone philosophy that engages primarily with that body of work.

subjects.term: Modern western and other noneastern philosophy
Philosophical traditions and schools of thought

data.name: Analytic Philosophy
data.description: Analytic philosophy is analyzes the use of language (linguistic turn) and, by clarity and rigor in its arguments, it focusses on solving philosophical questions. It contributes and utilizes formal logic and mathematics, and, to a lesser degree, the natural sciences.

data.name: German Idealism
data.description: German Idealism refers to a philosophical movement that emerged in Germany in the late 18th and early 19th centuries. It is characterized by a focus on the nature of consciousness, reason, and the relationship between mind and reality. German Idealism was a response to the Enlightenment and its emphasis on empirical science and rationalism. The central ideas and themes of German Idealism include: Transcendental idealism, Subjectivity and self-consciousness, Absolute idealism, Systematic philosophy.

subjects.term: Idealism and related systems and doctrines

data.name: Naturalism
data.description: Naturalism, in the social sciences and humanities, refers to a philosophical outlook that emphasizes the importance of empirical observation, analysis, and explanation, advocating for the use of scientific methods and the investigation of causality in understanding human behavior, culture, and society.

subjects.term: Naturalism and related systems and doctrines

data.name: Conceptual Analysis
data.description: Conceptual analysis is a philosophical methodology used to investigate the meaning and nature of concepts. It involves breaking down a concept into its constituent parts and examining how they relate to one another. The goal of conceptual analysis is to gain a deeper understanding of concepts and clarify their meanings, often in the context of philosophical or theoretical discussions.

data.name: Experimental Philosophy
data.description: Experimental philosophy is an interdisciplinary approach that combines philosophical inquiry with empirical research methods from psychology, cognitive science, and other disciplines. It seeks to investigate philosophical questions by gathering empirical data through experiments, surveys, and other empirical techniques, rather than relying solely on traditional philosophical methods such as conceptual analysis or logical argumentation.

subjects.term: Philosophy. Methodology. Relation to other topics

data.name: History of Philosophy as Method
data.description: The "history of philosophy as method" refers to an approach in philosophical inquiry where the study of the history of philosophy is seen as a methodological tool for engaging with philosophical questions. Rather than viewing the history of philosophy as a separate discipline or a mere historical survey, this approach considers it as an active and integral part of philosophical investigation.

subjects.term: Philosophical traditions and schools of thought

data.name: Logical Analysis
data.description: Logical analysis refers to the systematic examination and evaluation of arguments and propositions using the principles and methods of logic. It involves breaking down complex statements or arguments into their logical components to assess their validity, soundness, consistency, and coherence. Logical analysis aims to uncover the logical structure of a statement or argument and determine whether it follows valid reasoning.

data.name: Philosophy of Sociology
data.description: Philosophy of Sociology examines the foundational questions and theoretical frameworks of sociology, exploring the nature of social phenomena, knowledge, and methodologies.

subjects.term: Relation to social sciences. Relation to sociology

data.name: Numismatics
data.description: Numismatics is the study of coins, currency, and related objects, including their history, production, and cultural significance.

data.name: Sphragistics
data.description: Sphragistics, also known as sigillography, is the study of seals and signets, including their history, design, and use in authenticating documents and objects.

data.name: Heraldry
data.description: Heraldry studies the design and display of armorial bearings (known as armory).

data.name: Chronology
data.description: Chronology is the science of arranging events in their order of occurrence in time. It contains the methods, and systems of dating historical events, measuring the passage of time. Historiography can thus define temporal relationships between different occurrences.

data.name: Genealogy
data.description: Genealogy is the study of family history and lineage, tracing the ancestry and descent of individuals and families through historical records and genetic information.

data.name: Diplomatics
data.description: Diplomatics is a scholarly discipline centred on the critical analysis of documents – particularly, but not exclusively, historical documents.

data.name: Disability Pedagogy
data.description: Disability Pedagogy is the study and practice of inclusive teaching approaches that recognize disability as a form of human diversity, aiming to remove barriers and promote equitable learning for all students.

subjects.term: Teaching of students with physical impairments or disabilities

data.name: Special and Gifted Education
data.description: Gifted education (also known as gifted and talented education (GATE), talented and gifted programs (TAG), or G&T education) is a sort of education used for children who have been identified as gifted and talented.  The main approaches to gifted education are enrichment and acceleration. An enrichment program teaches additional, deeper material, but keeps the student progressing through the curriculum at the same rate as other students.  Special education (known as special-needs education, aided education, exceptional education, alternative provision, exceptional student education, special ed., SDC, or SPED) is the practice of educating students in a way that accommodates their individual differences, disabilities, and special needs. This involves the individually planned and systematically monitored arrangement of teaching procedures, adapted equipment and materials, and accessible settings. These interventions are designed to help individuals with special needs achieve a higher level of personal self-sufficiency and success in school and in their community, which may not be available if the student were only given access to a typical classroom education.

subjects.term: Teaching of specific groups & persons with special educational needs
Exceptional children and youth. Special education
Teaching of students with different educational needs

data.name: Experiential Education
data.description: Experiential education is an approach to learning that emphasizes direct engagement with real-world experiences as a means of acquiring knowledge, skills, and attitudes. It involves active participation, reflection, and application of learning in practical contexts, going beyond traditional classroom-based instruction.

data.name: Assessment and Testing
data.description: Assessment and testing are two related concepts in the field of education that focus on evaluating and measuring students' knowledge, skills, and understanding. Although they are interconnected, they have distinct meanings and purposes. Assessment refers to the ongoing process of gathering evidence and information about students' learning progress, achievements, and areas of growth. Testing, on the other hand, refers to a specific form of assessment that involves measuring students' knowledge and skills through standardized or formalized assessments.

subjects.term: Examinations and tests; academic prognosis and placement
Educational tests, measurements, evaluations and examinations

data.name: Holistic Education
data.description: Holistic education is an approach to learning that considers the whole person, focusing on the development of individuals intellectually, emotionally, socially, physically, and spiritually. It aims to cultivate well-rounded individuals who can thrive in various aspects of life and contribute positively to society. Holistic education goes beyond the traditional emphasis on academic achievement and incorporates a broader range of skills, values, and qualities.

data.name: Technology and Design education
data.description: Technology and Design Education is the study of teaching approaches and curriculum development with regards to the intersections of technology, engineering, and design, aiming to equip students with critical thinking, problem-solving, and technical skills.

data.name: Ultrasonics
data.description: Ultasonics are technological methods utilizing ultrasound. Ultrasound is sound waves with frequencies higher than the upper audible limit of human hearing.

data.name: African American Culture
data.description: African American culture is a subset of American culture, including literature, art, agricultural skills, cuisine, clothing styles, music and language specific to people with partial or total ancestry from Africa.

subjects.term: SOCIAL SCIENCE / Ethnic Studies / American / African American Studies

data.name: African Culture
data.description: The diverse culture of people from Africa, including music, language, art, food, religion, art and literature.

subjects.term: SOCIAL SCIENCE / Ethnic Studies / African Studies

data.name: American Culture
data.description: American Culture is formed of European American, Asian American, African American, Latin American, and Native American peoples and their cultures. The United States has its own distinct social and cultural characteristics, such as dialect, music, arts, social habits, cuisine, and folklore.

subjects.term: SOCIAL SCIENCE / Ethnic Studies / American / General

data.name: Asian Culture
data.description: Asian culture encompasses the collective and diverse customs and traditions of art, architecture, music, literature, lifestyle, philosophy, politics and religion that have been practiced and maintained by the numerous ethnic groups of the continent of Asia.

subjects.term: SOCIAL SCIENCE / Ethnic Studies / Asian Studies

data.name: Australasian Culture
data.description: Australasian Culture encompasses the collective and diverse customs and traditions of art, architecture, music, literature, lifestyle, philosophy, politics and religion that have been practiced and maintained by the numerous ethnic groups of the continent of Australia, New Zealand, New Guinea, and the neighbouring islands of the Pacific.

subjects.term: SOCIAL SCIENCE / Ethnic Studies / Australian & Oceanian Studies
Australasia, Oceania, Pacific Islands, Atlantic Islands

data.name: British Culture
data.description: The culture of Great Britain and the individual nations, England, Wales, Scotland, and Northern Ireland, which primarily includes literature and sport, along with film, television, food, and theatre.

subjects.term: SOCIAL SCIENCE / Ethnic Studies / European Studies

data.name: European Culture
data.description: The study of European culture - art, literature, history, film, philosophy, music, and architecture.

subjects.term: SOCIAL SCIENCE / Ethnic Studies / European Studies

data.name: Latin American Culture
data.description: Latin American culture is culture of the people of Latin America and includes literature, high art, popular culture, music, folk art, and dance, as well as religion and other customary practices.

subjects.term: SOCIAL SCIENCE / Ethnic Studies / Caribbean & Latin American Studies
Central and South America. Latin America (General)
Latin America – Mexico, Central America, South America

data.name: Latino Culture
data.description: Latino culture is an academic discipline which studies the culture of people born in Latin America and living in the United States.

subjects.term: SOCIAL SCIENCE / Ethnic Studies / American / Hispanic American Studies
Central and South America. Latin America (General)
Relating to Latin / Hispanic American people

data.name: Middle Eastern Culture
data.description: Studying the different cultural traditions and aspects of Middle Eastern and Arab countries.

subjects.term: SOCIAL SCIENCE / Ethnic Studies / Middle Eastern Studies
Near East. Middle East. Southwestern Asia

data.name: Global and International Culture
data.description: Global culture is a set of shared experiences, norms, symbols and ideas that unite people at the global level.

data.name: Digital Education and Educational Technology
data.description: Digital learning can take form in a blog, a video, a real-time lecture or seminar or even just an audio file. Digital learning will include at least one piece of technology such as a computer, laptop or mobile phone. One important definition of educational technology focuses on “the technological tools and media that assist in the communication of knowledge, and its development and exchange.” Take augmented reality and virtual reality, for example.

subjects.term: Educational equipment and technology, computer-aided learning (CAL)

data.name: Language Teaching and Learning
data.description: Language teaching and learning refers to the processes and practices involved in acquiring, teaching, and mastering a particular language. It encompasses various approaches, methods, and techniques used to facilitate language acquisition and proficiency development. Language teaching and learning can occur in formal educational settings, language schools, etc.

subjects.term: EDUCATION / Teaching Methods & Materials / Language Arts

data.name: Language Education
data.description: Language education refers to the field of teaching and learning languages, with a primary focus on developing proficiency in a specific language or languages. It encompasses various approaches, methods, and strategies used to facilitate language acquisition, communication skills, cultural understanding, and language proficiency.

subjects.term: EDUCATION / Teaching Methods & Materials / Language Arts

data.name: Literature Business
data.description: The term "business literature" encompasses the broad range of written materials that companies use to market their goods and services. Examples of business literature include publications as disparate as product catalogs, service brochures, and corporate newsletters.

subjects.term: Relation to sociology, economics, political science, etc. (social ideals, forces, etc. in literature)

data.name: Ecocriticism
data.description: Ecocriticism is the study of literature and ecology from an interdisciplinary point of view, where literature scholars analyze texts that illustrate environmental concerns and examine the various ways literature treats the subject of nature.

subjects.term: Literature dealing with specific themes and subjects--economics

data.name: Intermediality
data.description: Intermediality, in other words, is not only the general term that defines the relationships between autonomous media, it is also the term that identifies the internal plurality of each medium. The intermedial study of literature therefore does not only refer to the study of the relationships between the literary text and its “others” (for instance the illustrations that accompany it, to give an elementary example), it also includes the study of the literary as a heterogeneous material that conveys a more or less radical “semiotic rupture” within itself (for instance when we interpret aspects of typography, from typeface to page layout and book design, as aspects of the text’s visuality—a dimension of literature that has always been at the center of visual and experimental poetry).

data.name: Classical Music
data.description: Though "classical music" is the vernacular term, the more accepted academic term is "concert music" or "Western art music." There are many kinds of "classical" musics--e.g., Indian classical music, European classical music--though the term tends to refer primarily to music rooted in the European art music tradition of the 17th-19th centuries.

subjects.term: Art music, orchestral and formal music

data.name: Contemporary Music
data.description: Contemporary music typically refers to avant-garde art music of the late 20th and early 21st century; it is sometimes called "New Music."

data.name: History of Music
data.description: Musicology has traditionally focused on the history of music, though in the last 40 years it has expanded to include cultural studies and critical theory methodologies.

data.name: Jazz
data.description: Jazz is a genre of popular music rooted in 20th century African-American urban musical communities and often incorporating improvisation. There are many sub-genres of jazz, including free jazz, fusion, swing, bop and hard bop, neoclassical, etc.

data.name: Music Theatre
data.description: Musical Theatre includes popular and avant-garde theatrical productions and screen musicals that combine acting and singing.

data.name: Pop and Rock
data.description: Pop and Rock refers to both rock-and-roll based popular musics and pop music as a genre that can include but expands beyond rock and roll, often to include a multi-genre mix of music from multiple ethnic and racial groups. The emphasis is commercial rather than underground or indie. When in reference to radio, "pop and rock" generally refers to formats such as "contemporary hits" or "adult hits."

data.name: Popular Music
data.description: Popular music includes music of any genre that has been dubbed or considered popular in any geographic region and at any time in history. It can include pop, rock, EDM, hip hop, folk, blues, jazz, and also things like Broadway musicals and film musicals.

data.name: Theory of Music
data.description: Music Theory focuses on the technical analysis of musical compositions, breaking down their form, harmony, melody, rhythm, timbre, dynamics, and other musical elements. Newer methods include spectrogram analysis and work in music cognition.

subjects.term: Philosophy and theory, analytical guides, program notes

data.name: Radio
data.description: Radio studies explores radio culture and the radio industry, the meaning of radio, both for the individual listener and for its place in wider society. Includes the study of acoustics, public service broadcasting, DJs, radio dramas, phone-ins, talk radio, radio advertising, internet and digital radio, news and much more.

data.name: Mathematics Education
data.description: In contemporary education, mathematics education—known in Europe as the didactics or pedagogy of mathematics—is the practice of teaching, learning, and carrying out scholarly research into the transfer of mathematical knowledge.  Although research into mathematics education is primarily concerned with the tools, methods, and approaches that facilitate practice or the study of practice, it also covers an extensive field of study encompassing a variety of different concepts, theories and methods. National and international organisations regularly hold conferences and publish literature in order to improve mathematics education.

data.name: History of Sociology
data.description: The history of sociology traces the development of sociological ideas, theories, and methods from their origins to the present day. This field examines the foundations of sociology as an academic discipline, its evolution over time, the contributions of key thinkers and scholars, and the impact of historical events and social contexts on the course of sociological inquiry.

subjects.term: History of sociology. History of sociological theory

data.name: Sociology of Science
data.description: Sociology of science examines the social processes, institutions, and dynamics involved in the production, dissemination, and reception of scientific knowledge, including the role of scientific communities, funding, and public perception of science.

data.name: Deviance and Social Control
data.description: Deviance is any behavior that violates the norms of a society. Crime is a form of deviance that is considered to be so serious that is penalized by local laws. Social control involves the ways in which societies try to control deviant behavior.

data.name: Formal Logic
data.description: Formal logic is the process of using logical rules and principles to derive valid conclusions from a set of premises, often represented by mathematical or symbolic notation. It is used in disciplines such as logic, mathematics, and computer science.

data.name: Palaeography
data.description: Palaeography is the study of historical handwriting, focusing on deciphering and interpreting the script, style, and context of written documents to understand their historical significance and dating. It plays a crucial role in deciphering ancient manuscripts and understanding the development of writing systems over time.

data.name: History of Ideas
data.description: History of Ideas explores the development and transformation of key concepts, philosophies, and intellectual movements throughout history, examining their impact on culture and society.

data.name: Corporate History
data.description: A corporate history is a historical account of a business or other co-operative organization. Usually it is produced in written format but it can also be published as audio or audiovisually.

subjects.term: History of specific companies / corporate history
History of specific companies / corporate history

data.name: Church History
data.description: Church History studies the development, organization, and influence of Christian churches and denominations over time, including their theological, social, and cultural impacts.

subjects.term: History, geographic treatment, biography of Christianity

data.name: Lexicology / Vocabulary
data.description: Lexicology is the branch of linguistics that analyzes the lexicon of a specific language. A word is the smallest meaningful unit of a language that can stand on its own, and is made up of small components called morphemes and even smaller elements known as phonemes, or distinguishing sounds. Lexicology examines every feature of a word – including formation, spelling, origin, usage, and definition.

subjects.term: Communication; semantics, pragmatics, languages for special purposes

data.name: Phonology and Phonetics
data.description: Phonetics deals with the production of speech sounds by humans, often without prior knowledge of the language being spoken. Phonology is about patterns of sounds, especially different patterns of sounds in different languages, or within each language, different patterns of sounds in different positions in words etc.

subjects.term: LANGUAGE ARTS & DISCIPLINES / Linguistics / Phonetics & Phonology
Phonology and phonetics of standard forms of languages

data.name: Pragmatics
data.description: In linguistics and related fields, pragmatics is the study of how context contributes to meaning. The field of study evaluates how human language is utilized in social interactions, as well as the relationship between the interpreter and the interpreted.

data.name: Orthography
data.description: An orthography is a set of conventions for writing a language, including norms of spelling, hyphenation, capitalization, word boundaries, emphasis, and punctuation.

subjects.term: Writing systems of standard forms of languages

data.name: Graphemics
data.description: Graphemics or graphematics is the linguistic study of writing systems and their basic components, i.e. graphemes.

subjects.term: Writing systems of standard forms of languages

data.name: Psycholinguistics and Cognitive Linguistics
data.description: Psycholinguistics and Cognitive Linguistics investigates the psychological processes involved in the use of language and the influence of language in our cognitive interaction with the world. It includes language comprehension, language production, and first and second language acquisition as well as linguistic analysis and the perspectival nature of meaning.

subjects.term: Psychological principles, language acquisition, speech perception

data.name: Celtic
data.description: Celtic refers to a group of related languages and cultures that were historically spoken by Celtic peoples across parts of Western Europe. The Celtic language family is divided into two main branches: Continental Celtic and Insular Celtic.

data.name: Uralic-Altaic Languages
data.description: The classification of Uralic-Altaic as a language family combining Uralic and Altaic languages is a matter of debate among linguists. The Altaic language family hypothesis suggests a connection between the Turkic, Mongolic, and Tungusic languages, while the Uralic language family includes languages such as Finnish, Hungarian, Estonian, and others.

subjects.term: Altaic, Uralic, Hyperborean, Dravidian languages, miscellaneous languages of south Asia

data.name: Agronomy
data.description: Agronomy is the science and technology of producing and using plants by agriculture for food, fuel, fiber, chemicals, recreation, or land conservation. Agronomy has come to include research of plant genetics, plant physiology, meteorology, and soil science. Agronomists work to optimize crop production by studying plant genetics, soil fertility, crop rotation, irrigation, pest management, and other factors that affect plant growth and productivity.

data.name: Socio-Legal Studies
data.description: Socio-Legal Studies is an interdisciplinary field that combines elements of sociology and law to examine the social and cultural aspects of legal systems, legal processes, and the relationship between law and society. It focuses on understanding how law operates in practice, how it shapes social behavior, and how social factors influence legal processes and outcomes.

subjects.term: Law and society, sociology of law

data.name: Philosophy of the Self
data.description: The philosophy of the self is a branch of philosophy that investigates the nature, existence, and significance of the self or personal identity. It explores questions about the nature of the self, its relation to the mind and body, its continuity over time, and its role in human experience and agency.

data.name: Medieval Philosophy
data.description: Medieval Philosophy, also known as Scholastic Philosophy, refers to the philosophical thought and intellectual developments that took place in Europe during the Middle Ages, from the 5th to the 15th century. It was heavily influenced by Christian theology and the works of ancient Greek and Roman philosophers.

subjects.term: Western philosophy: Medieval & Renaissance, c 500 to c 1600

data.name: Renaissance Philosophy
data.description: Renaissance Philosophy refers to the philosophical thought and intellectual developments that took place during the Renaissance period in Europe, spanning roughly from the 14th to the 17th century. It was a time of renewed interest in classical Greek and Roman philosophy, literature, and culture, and it marked a shift away from the dominant religious and scholastic traditions of the Middle Ages.

subjects.term: Western philosophy: Medieval & Renaissance, c 500 to c 1600

data.name: Early Modern Philosophy
data.description: Early Modern Philosophy refers to the period of philosophy that emerged in the 17th and 18th centuries, following the Renaissance and preceding the Enlightenment. This period marked a significant shift in philosophical thought and laid the foundation for many contemporary philosophical ideas.

subjects.term: Philosophical traditions and schools of thought

data.name: Physics Phenomenology
data.description: Physics Phenomenology is the application of theoretical physics to experimental data by making quantitative predictions based upon known theories. In particle physics, it forms a bridge between the mathematical models of theoretical physics and the results of the high-energy particle experiments.

data.name: Space Exploration and Astronautics
data.description: Space exploration is the use of astronomy and space technology to explore outer space. While the exploration of space is carried out mainly by astronomers with telescopes, its physical exploration is conducted both by uncrewed robotic space probes and human spaceflight. Space exploration, like its classical form astronomy, is one of the main sources for space science.

data.name: Newtonian Physics
data.description: Newtonian physics, also called Newtonian or classical mechanics, is the description of mechanical events—those that involve forces acting on matter—using the laws of motion and gravitation formulated in the late seventeenth century by English physicist Sir Isaac Newton

subjects.term: Theories of gravitation (Including antigravity, quantum gravity)

data.name: Alternative Relativity
data.description: Alternatives to general relativity are physical theories that attempt to describe the phenomenon of gravitation in competition to Einstein's theory of general relativity. There have been many different attempts at constructing an ideal theory of gravity

subjects.term: Theories of gravitation (Including antigravity, quantum gravity)

data.name: Continuum Mechanics
data.description: Continuum mechanics deals with the mechanical behavior of materials and fluids modeled as a continuous mass rather than as discrete particles.

data.name: Food Analysis
data.description: Food analysis is a diverse and interdisciplinary field of research that has a significant health, societal and economic impact. It aims to characterize food products in terms of chemical composition, traceability, safety, quality, sensory perception and nutritional value.

subjects.term: TECHNOLOGY & ENGINEERING / Food Science / Chemistry & Biotechnology

data.name: Food Engineering
data.description: Food engineering is a scientific, academic, and professional field that interprets and applies principles of engineering, science, and mathematics to food manufacturing and operations, including the processing, production, handling, storage, conservation, control, packaging and distribution of food products.

data.name: Food Safety
data.description: Food safety is used as a scientific discipline describing handling, preparation, and storage of food in ways that prevent food-borne illness.

subjects.term: TECHNOLOGY & ENGINEERING / Food Science / Food Safety & Security

data.name: Sensory Evaluation
data.description: Sensory evaluation is a scientific discipline used to evoke, measure, analyze, and interpret reaction to those characteristics of food material as they are perceived by the senses of sight, smell, taste, touch, and hearing (sound).

subjects.term: TECHNOLOGY & ENGINEERING / Food Science / Chemistry & Biotechnology

data.name: Bioinspired Technologies
data.description: Development and application of technologies that are inspired by or mimic biological systems, processes, or principles found in nature

subjects.term: Auxiliary techniques and procedures; apparatus, equipment, materials

data.name: Biomechanical Analysis and Modeling
data.description: Biomechanical analysis and modeling involve studying the mechanical behavior and properties of biological systems, such as cells, tissues, organs, and organisms. These approaches combine principles of engineering, physics, and biology to understand how forces and mechanics influence biological structures and functions. Biomechanical analysis and modeling play a crucial role in various fields, including biomechanics, sports science, orthopedics, rehabilitation, and biomedical engineering.

subjects.term: Auxiliary techniques and procedures; apparatus, equipment, materials

data.name: Biomedical Devices and Instrumentation
data.description: Biomedical devices and instrumentation refer to the tools, equipment, and systems used in the field of biomedical engineering and healthcare to diagnose, monitor, treat, or assist in the management of medical conditions. These devices and instruments are designed to interface with biological systems, provide accurate measurements, deliver therapeutic interventions, or aid in the analysis of biological samples.

subjects.term: Auxiliary techniques and procedures; apparatus, equipment, materials

data.name: Gerontology
data.description: Gerontolotgy comprises the sociological aspects of elderly individuals' lives. Furthermore it addresses cultural, psychological, cognitive, and biological aspects of ageing and an aging population.

data.name: Social Justice
data.description: Social justice is a concept of fair and just relations between the individual and society, as measured by the distribution of wealth, opportunities for personal activity, and social privileges.

subjects.term: SOCIAL SCIENCE / Social Classes & Economic Disparity

data.name: Animal Science
data.description: An animal scientist applies principles of the biological, physical, and social sciences to the problems associated with livestock production and management.

data.name: Veterinary Clinical Medicine
data.description: Veterinary Clinical Medicine is the branch of medicine that deals with the causes, diagnosis, and treatment of diseases and injuries of animals, especially domestic animals.

data.name: Risk Management
data.description: Risk management is a corporate finance field that focuses on identifying, assessing, and managing risks that could impact the financial performance and stability of a business. It involves the development and implementation of strategies and processes that can help an organization mitigate risks and minimize potential losses. In corporate finance, risk management typically involves the identification and analysis of financial risks, such as credit risk, market risk, liquidity risk, and operational risk. The aim is to manage these risks to ensure that the organization can achieve its financial objectives while minimizing losses and maintaining financial stability. Risk management in corporate finance also involves regulatory compliance, ensuring that the organization adheres to regulatory requirements and guidelines related to risk management practices. This includes establishing risk management policies and procedures, implementing internal controls, and reporting on risk management activities to stakeholders. The field of risk management in corporate finance has become increasingly important in recent years due to the increasing complexity of financial markets, changing regulatory requirements, and the need for businesses to manage risks effectively in order to remain competitive and achieve sustainable growth.

subjects.term: BUSINESS & ECONOMICS / Finance / Financial Risk Management

data.name: Medical Physics
data.description: Medical Physics is a branch of Applied Physics, pursued by medical physicists, that uses physics principles, methods and techniques in practice and research for the prevention, diagnosis and treatment of human diseases with a specific goal of improving human health and well-being.

subjects.term: Medical physics. Medical radiology. Nuclear medicine

data.name: Operating Systems
data.description: An operating system (OS) is system software that manages computer hardware and software resources, and provides common services for computer programs. Also, it serves as the point of communication or interface between a user and the computer's hardware.

data.name: Compilers and Interpreters
data.description: A compiler is a special program that translates a programming language's source code into machine code while An interpreter is a program that directly executes the instructions in a high-level language, without converting it into machine code.

data.name: C++
data.description: C++ is a widely used programming language that is known for its versatility and efficiency. It is an extension of the C programming language and supports both procedural and object-oriented programming paradigms.

data.name: Lisp
data.description: Lisp programming language, Common Lisp. Lisp, short for "List Processing," is a high-level programming language known for its unique and distinctive syntax and its powerful support for symbolic data manipulation and functional programming.  It was designed to be a practical tool for artificial intelligence (AI) research, and its strong emphasis on symbolic computation and recursion made it an ideal choice for processing symbolic data and solving complex problems.

data.name: Perl
data.description: Perl is a high-level, general-purpose programming language known for its versatility, flexibility, and powerful text-processing capabilities. Perl stands for "Practical Extraction and Reporting Language," but it is also known as the "Pathologically Eclectic Rubbish Lister" due to its various and eclectic features.

data.name: Communication Psychology
data.description: Communication psychology is a field of psychology that focuses on the study of how individuals perceive, interpret, and engage in communication processes. It examines the psychological factors that influence communication effectiveness, including verbal and nonverbal communication, interpersonal dynamics, and the impact of media on human communication.

data.name: Biochemistry
data.description: Biochemistry is the scientific study of the chemical structures, processes, and interactions that occur within living organisms. It examines the chemistry of biomolecules and the regulation of biochemical pathways within and between cells. The field focuses on fundamental molecular mechanisms such as metabolism, enzyme function, protein structure, nucleic acids, and cellular signaling in all forms of life, including animals, plants, and microorganisms.

data.name: Agent-based Economics
data.description: Agent-based computational economics (ACE) is the area of computational economics that studies economic processes, including whole economies, as dynamic systems of interacting agents. As such, it falls in the paradigm of complex adaptive systems.

data.name: Feminist Economics
data.description: Feminist economics is the critical study of economics and economies, with a focus on gender-aware and inclusive economic inquiry and policy analysis. Feminist economic researchers include academics, activists, policy theorists, and practitioners. Much feminist economic research focuses on topics that have been neglected in the field, such as care work, intimate partner violence, or on economic theories which could be improved through better incorporation of gendered effects and interactions, such as between paid and unpaid sectors of economies.

data.name: Marxist Economics
data.description: Marxian economics is a school of economic thought based on the work of 19th-century economist and philosopher Karl Marx. Marxian economics, or Marxist economics, focuses on the role of labor in the development of an economy and is critical of the classical approach to wages and productivity developed by Adam Smith.

data.name: Auditing
data.description: Auditing is a systematic and independent examination of an entity's financial statements, records, and other relevant information to provide an opinion on their accuracy and reliability. The primary objective of auditing is to enhance the credibility of financial information provided to stakeholders by identifying and addressing material misstatements, errors, and fraud.  In research, auditing involves the development and testing of theories related to the audit process, audit quality, and the impact of auditing on financial reporting and decision-making. The field of auditing research covers a wide range of topics, including audit risk, audit evidence, audit regulation, auditor independence, and audit market competition.  Audit risk refers to the risk that the auditor will issue an incorrect opinion on an entity's financial statements, which could result in stakeholders making incorrect decisions based on unreliable information. Audit evidence refers to the information used by the auditor to support their opinion on the accuracy and reliability of an entity's financial statements.  Audit regulation refers to the rules and standards that govern the conduct of auditors and the performance of audits. Auditor independence refers to the ability of the auditor to provide an objective and unbiased opinion on an entity's financial statements, free from any conflicts of interest or undue influence.  Audit market competition refers to the level of competition among audit firms and how it affects audit quality and pricing.  In practice, auditing involves the examination of an entity's financial statements and records, the testing of internal controls, and the evaluation of management's representations. The auditor uses various techniques and procedures, including sampling, analytical procedures, and substantive testing, to gather sufficient and appropriate evidence to support their opinion.  Auditing is typically performed by certified public accountants (CPAs) who are independent of the entity being audited. The result of an audit is typically a report that includes the auditor's opinion on the accuracy and reliability of the entity's financial statements.

data.name: Social Work Policy
data.description: Social work policy is a field of study within social work that focuses on the development, analysis, and evaluation of social policies and their impact on individuals, families, groups, and communities. It involves examining the social, political, and economic factors that shape policies, advocating for social justice and equity, and promoting policies that address social issues and promote social well-being.

It involves the application of research methods and techniques to generate knowledge that contributes to evidence-based practice and social change.

data.description: Soft and Granular Matter is a granular material which is a multiphase material made up of a large collection of closely packed solid particles surrounded by a gas or a liquid. Because the ratio of the volume of solid to fluid phases is very high, the particles are in very close contact with each other.

data.name: Legislative Politics
data.description: Legislative Politics examines the functioning, behavior, and decision-making processes of legislative bodies, including the roles of legislators, committees, and political parties in lawmaking.

data.name: Psychosocial Studies
data.description: Psychosocial Studies examines the social influences on individual behavior. It seeks to investigate the ways in which psychic and social processes can be understood as implicated in each other and mutually constitutive.

data.name: Grammar
data.description: Grammar is the systematic study and set of rules that govern the structure of language, including the formation of words, phrases, and sentences. It encompasses the principles that dictate syntax, morphology, and phonology, enabling clear and meaningful communication.

data.name: Homological Algebra
data.description: Homological algebra is the branch of mathematics that studies homology in a general algebraic setting. It is the study of homological functors and the intricate algebraic structures that they entail

data.name: Museology
data.description: Museum studies is the study of museums. It explores the history of museums and their role in society, as well as the activities they engage in, including curating, preservation, public programming, and education.

data.name: Fashion Business
data.description: "Fashion Business" refers to the industry and commercial activities involved in the design, production, marketing, and retailing of clothing, accessories, and footwear.

data.name: Urban Education
data.description: Urban education refers to the field of study, practice, and policy focused on the educational needs of students and communities in metropolitan areas, especially inner cities. It involves understanding the unique challenges and opportunities present in these contexts, including issues of diversity, poverty, and access to quality education.

data.name: Rural Education
data.description: Rural education encompasses the schooling provided in areas with low population density, often facing distinct challenges and advantages compared to urban and suburban counterparts.

data.name: Health Policy and Systems Research
data.description: Health policy and systems research (HPSR) is an interdisciplinary field that studies how societies organize to achieve their health goals, focusing on the policies, organizations, people, and interactions that make up a health system.

data.name: Metallurgy
data.description: Metallurgy is the branch of science and engineering concerned with the properties of metals and their production, processing, and performance. It involves: Extracting metals from ores  Refining and alloying metals to achieve desired properties Shaping and treating metals through processes like casting, forging, rolling, and heat treatment Studying the structure and behavior of metals at the atomic and microscopic levels to improve strength, durability, corrosion resistance, etc.

data.name: JavaScript
data.description: JavaScript is a high-level, interpreted programming language primarily used to create interactive and dynamic content on websites. It runs in web browsers and enables features like animations, form validation, and real-time updates.

data.name: Product Design and Prototyping
data.description: Product Design is the process of conceptualizing, designing, testing, and refining products,  digital services, or experiences to solve user problems

data.name: Rust
data.description: Rust is a general purpose programming language designed for safety, speed, and concurrency. It eliminates typical programming errors like memory leaks and data races.

data.name: Transitional Economics
data.description: The study of economies that move from one economic system to another. This is an area of study that developed following the end of the Soviet Union and the shift from centrally planned economies to market economies seen within the ex-Soviet states. Other countries that have also shifted economic systems, such as China and countries in South America, have also been areas of focus.

data.name: Creative Industries
data.description: Creative industries are those industries which have their origin in individual creativity, skill and talent which have a potential for job and wealth creation through the generation and exploitation of intellectual property"Examples of creative industries include music, the arts and theatre.

data.name: Semantics
data.description: Semantics is the study of reference, meaning, or truth.

data.name: Public Sector
data.description: The public sector, also called the state sector, is the part of the economy composed of both public services and public enterprises. Public sectors include the public goods and governmental services such as the military, law enforcement, public infrastructure, public transit, public education, along with public health care and those working for the government itself, such as elected officials.

data.name: Natural Resource Economics
data.description: Natural Resource Economics is the study of how societies use and manage the Earth's natural resources—such as water, minerals, forests, and energy—in ways that balance economic needs with environmental sustainability.

data.name: Materials Modelling
data.description: Materials modelling refers to theoretical and computational methods and models used to understand, simulate and predict material behaviour

data.name: Materials Design
data.description: Materials design is the systematic development of materials with targeted properties using modelling, experimental methods, and optimization strategies

data.name: Statistical Learning
data.description: Statistical learning is the study of how to understand, model, and predict patterns in data using both probabilistic theory and algorithmic methods. It covers a spectrum from classical statistical models to modern machine‑learning techniques that learn structure from data.

data.name: Educational Policy and Politics
data.description: Educational policy and politics refer to the processes, decisions, and actions related to the development, implementation, and evaluation of policies that shape the educational system. It involves the intersection of educational goals, societal needs, political agendas, and the allocation of resources. Educational policy and politics influence various aspects of education, including curriculum, funding, assessment, teacher training, school governance, and educational equity.

data.name: Children's Rights
data.description: Children's rights encompass the basic freedoms and protections that all children should have, such as the right to education, health care, a safe living environment, and the freedom from abuse, exploitation, and discrimination. These rights are enshrined in international treaties like the United Nations Convention on the Rights of the Child (UNCRC), which emphasizes that children have the right to be heard, to have their best interests considered, and to develop to their fullest potential. Essentially, it's about ensuring every child can thrive and grow in a supportive and nurturing environment.

data.name: Decolonization
data.description: Decolonisation refers to the process through which colonies become independent from colonial powers, involving the dismantling of colonial structures and ideologies. It's both a political and cultural journey, aiming to reclaim Indigenous identities, autonomy, and governance. It also involves addressing the lingering impacts of colonisation, including social and economic inequalities, and often calls for a re-evaluation of historical narratives and power dynamics.

data.name: Intersectionality
data.description: Intersectionality is a framework for understanding how various forms of social stratification—like race, gender, class, and others—overlap and intersect, creating complex and unique systems of discrimination and privilege. Coined by Kimberlé Crenshaw in 1989, it emphasizes that people's experiences can't be understood by looking at social categories in isolation; instead, we need to consider how these categories interact and influence each other.

data.name: Cultural Management
data.description: Cultural management refers to the professional planning, organization, and control of cultural activities and institutions. It encompasses strategic development, financing, personnel management, marketing, as well as the operational management of cultural projects, facilities, or events with the aim of efficiently utilizing cultural resources and making cultural content accessible to a (broad) audience. Central reference disciplines include business administration management theory, cultural and theatre studies, cultural policy, cultural sociology, and cultural economics.

data.name: Political Ideology
data.description: Political Ideology refers to a set of beliefs and values about the goals and organization of society, guiding political behavior and policy preferences, including ideologies such as liberalism, conservatism, and socialism.

data.name: Mathematical Biology
data.description: Mathematical biology or biomathematics is a branch of biology which employs theoretical analysis, mathematical models and abstractions of the living organisms to investigate the principles that govern the structure, development and behavior of the systems, as opposed to experimental biology which deals with the conduction of experiments to prove and validate the scientific theories.

data.name: Tissues
data.description: Tissues are ensembles of similar or compatible types of animal or plant cells that together carry out a specific function. In the human body there are four categories of tissues: epithelial, connective, nervous and muscle.

data.name: Horticulture
data.description: Horticulture is the branch of agriculture that focuses on the cultivation, production, and management of garden plants, including fruits, vegetables, nuts, seeds, herbs, mushrooms, algae, flowers, seaweeds, and non-food crops such as grass and ornamental trees and plants. It encompasses a wide range of activities, including plant breeding, crop production, landscape design, and pest management, and integrates principles from botany, soil science, and environmental science. Horticulturists apply scientific knowledge and techniques to improve plant growth, yield, quality, and sustainability, often utilizing innovative practices such as hydroponics, organic farming, and integrated pest management. The field plays a crucial role in food security, environmental conservation, and enhancing the aesthetic and functional value of urban and rural landscapes.

data.name: Oral Diseases

data.name: Reaction Mechanism

data.name: Haematological Diseases
data.description: Haematological diseases are pathological conditions primarily affecting the blood or blood-producing organs. This group of disorders includes, but is not limited to, various types of anaemia, blood cancers and haemorrhagic conditions.

subjects.term: Diseases of the blood and blood-forming organs. Hematologic diseases

data.name: Cancers
data.description: Cancer is a complex disease in which cells in a specific tissue are no longer fully responsive to the signals within the tissue that regulate cellular differentiation, survival, proliferation and death. As a result, these cells accumulate within the tissue, causing local damage and inflammation. There are over 200 different types of cancer.

data.name: Networks and Systems Biology
data.description: Networks and systems biology is the study of complex systems by a holistic approach where the 'omics approaches such as transcriptomics, glycomics and lipidomics find wide use. Networks and systems biology aims to understand the networks of interactions and effects of those interactions on a global scale, involving hundreds of different biological molecules simultaneously.

data.name: Cardiovascular Diseases
data.description: Cardiovascular diseases are pathological conditions affecting the heart and/or blood vessels, that is, the cardiovascular system.

data.name: Bacteria
data.description: Bacteria are organisms that consist of a single cell without a nucleus and with distinct structural, physiological and evolutionary characteristics. Bacteria form one of the three domains of life; the others are archaea and eukaryotes. Bacterial species and their habitats exhibit great diversity.

data.name: Neurodevelopmental Disorders

data.name: Neuronal Development
data.description: Neuronal development is the biological process by which neurons are produced during development. The processes that contribute to neuronal development include proliferation, differentiation, migration, axon guidance and synapse formation.

data.name: Neurological Disorders
data.description: Neurological disorders are disorders that affect the central nervous system or the peripheral nervous systems and can impair the brain, spinal cord, peripheral nerve or neuromuscular function.

data.name: Religion and Health
data.description: Scholarly studies have investigated the effects of religion on health. The World Health Organization (WHO) discerns four dimensions of health, namely physical, social, mental, and spiritual health. Having a religious belief may have both positive and negative impacts on health and morbidity.

data.name: Rheumatic Diseases
data.description: Rheumatic diseases is an umbrella term that encompasses the spectrum of musculoskeletal, arthritic and connective tissue disorders.

data.name: Lipids
data.description: Lipids are hydrophobic or amphiphilic small molecules that include sterols, waxes, fatty acids and phospholipids, and are insoluble in water and soluble in organic solvent. Biological lipids are generated from ketoacyl and isoprene (CH2=C(CH3)CH=CH2) groups and include glycerolipids, sphingolipids, fatty acids and polyketides. Lipids play roles in energy storage, signalling and as structural components.

data.name: Genome
data.description: The genome is the full genetic complement of an organism, encoded in either DNA or, in many viruses, RNA. It includes both the genes and non-coding sequences.

data.name: Immune System
data.description: The immune system is a complex network of cells, tissues and organs that work together to protect the body from harmful substances and organisms and defend against disease. The immune system can be classified into distinct responses, such as innate immunity and adaptive immunity, or humoral immunity and cell-mediated immunity.

data.name: Data Science
data.description: Data science is an interdisciplinary academic field that uses statistics, scientific computing, scientific methods, processes, algorithms and systems to extract or extrapolate knowledge and insights from noisy, structured, and unstructured data.

data.name: Disease Prevention
data.description: Disease prevention is a procedure through which individuals, particularly those with risk factors for a disease, are treated in order to prevent a disease from occurring. Treatment normally begins either before signs and symptoms of the disease occur, or shortly thereafter. Treatment can include patient education, lifestyle modification, and drugs.

data.name: DNA Nanotechnology
data.description: DNA nanotechnology is a branch of nanotechnology concerned with the design, study and application of synthetic structures based on DNA. DNA nanotechnology takes advantage of the physical and chemical properties of DNA rather than the genetic information it carries.

data.name: Nanomaterial
data.description: Nanomaterials and Nanostructures are structures that range between 1 nm (molecular scale) and 100 nm in at least one dimension. Most are synthetic and can be engineered to wide range of physical properties. Nanosurfaces, nanowires, cylindrical nanotubes, nanospheres etc. are common nanostructured materials.

data.description: Endocrine systems and metabolic diseases affect the endocrine system and disrupt metabolism. Examples include diabetes and goiter.

data.description: The development and application of optical techniques, particularly imaging, to the study of biological molecules, cells and tissue.

data.name: Policing
data.description: Policing ocuses on the study of law enforcement agencies, their practices, policies, and strategies for maintaining public order, preventing crime, and ensuring community safety. It examines the role of police officers, the organization and structure of police departments, and the relationships between the police and the communities they serve. Policing in criminology encompasses various aspects, such as community policing, police discretion, use of force, accountability, and the impact of policing on crime and public trust.

data.name: Gene Therapy
data.description: Gene therapy involves the introduction of new genes into cells, to restore or add gene expression, for the purpose of treating disease. Most commonly a mutated gene is replaced with DNA encoding a functional copy. Alternatively DNA encoding a therapeutic protein drug may be introduced.

data.name: Entosis
data.description: Entosis is a process by which one cell invades or is engulfed by another cell. Unlike the clearance of apoptotic cells by phagocytosis, the internalised cell is initially alive.

data.name: Biofuels
data.description: Biofuels are fuels produced from hydrocarbon-rich living organisms (biomass) — such as plants or microalgae — by thermal, chemical or biochemical conversion processes. As with fuels, biofuels such as biodiesel, biogas and syngas are combusted to generate energy.

data.name: Development Finance
data.description: Development finance is a subset of economics comprising hypotheses and practices on how to efficiently allocate resources towards economic and social transformation (development) of entire nations. It was born out of the challenge to promote the rapid economic transformation (development) of newly independent nations, and to reconstruct former industrial economies destroyed, physically and economically, by the two great wars of the twentieth century.

data.name: Political Economy of Energy
data.description: Political Economy of Energy studies all aspects of energy in relation to law, customs and government.

data.name: Systems Virology
data.description: Systems virology is the scientific discipline that integrates high-throughput molecular techniques and computational tools to study all aspects of viruses and viral diseases, in an effort to increase our understanding of viral pathogenesis and to improve diagnostics and therapeutics of viral diseases.

data.name: Motivated Behavior
data.description: One general aspect of motivated behaviors is that they lead to a goal and obtaining the goal is rewarding. Thus, motivation, defined as the energizing of behavior in pursuit of a goal, is a fundamental property of all deliberative behaviors.

data.name: Urogenital Disorders
data.description: Urogenital disorders are diseases and abnormalities affecting the urinary system (kidneys, ureters, bladder, urethra) and the reproductive organs, including infectious, congenital, neoplastic, inflammatory, and functional conditions.

data.name: Protein Biochemistry
data.description: Protein biochemistry is the study of proteins. It encompasses several fields, including molecular biology, cell biology, pharmaceutical discovery and crosses over from eukaryotic cells (animal and plant cells) to prokaryotic cells (bacteria and archaea cells).

data.name: Genetic Predisposition to Disease
data.description: Genetic predisposition to disease is a latent susceptibility to a disease phenotype at the genetic level. Development of the disease is not certain; it's appearance and severity is influenced by other conditions.

data.name: Fluorescent Dyes
data.description: Fluorescent dyes are non-protein molecules that absorb light and re-emit it at a longer wavelength. They are often used in the fluorescent labelling of biomolecules and can be smaller or more photostable than fluorescent proteins but cannot be genetically encoded.

data.name: Bariatric Surgery
data.description: Bariatric surgery is a type of surgery performed on morbidly obese individuals to achieve weight loss. Established procedures include Roux-en-Y gastric bypass, laparoscopic adjustable gastric band, biliopancreatic diversion with duodenal switch and sleeve gastrectomy.

data.name: RNA modification
data.description: RNA modifications are changes to the chemical composition of ribonucleic acid (RNA) molecules post-synthesis that have the potential to alter function or stability. An example of RNA modification is the addition of a methylated guanine nucleotide “cap” to the 5’-end of messenger RNAs (mRNAs).

data.name: Kidney Diseases
data.description: Kidney diseases are hereditary and nonhereditary disorders that affect the kidney. Diabetes mellitus and high blood pressure are important risk factors for kidney disease.

data.name: Genetic Interaction
data.description: Genetic interaction is the phenomenon where the effects of one gene are modified by one or several other genes.

data.name: Technological Innovation
data.description: A technological innovation is a new or improved product or process whose technological characteristics are significantly different from before. Implemented technological product innovations are new products (product innovations) or processes in application (process innovations) that have been brought to market.

data.name: Adrenal Glands
data.description: The adrenal glands are two endocrine glands found just above the kidneys that consist of two distinct layers. The cortex layer secretes steroid hormones, such as testosterone and cortisol, whereas the medulla layer secretes adrenaline and noradrenaline.

data.name: Insurance
data.description: The insurance industry is a field of business and management research that focuses on the study of the insurance sector. This includes the analysis of various types of insurance products such as life insurance, health insurance, property and casualty insurance, and other specialized insurance products. Research in this field covers a range of topics, including the regulation of the industry, risk management, underwriting, claims processing, and actuarial science. Additionally, research may examine the impact of emerging technologies on the industry, the use of big data and analytics, and the role of insurance in broader economic and social contexts.

data.name: Cytokines and Growth Factors
data.description: Cytokines are proteins, peptides or glycoproteins secreted by lymphocytes and monocytes that regulate immune responses, haematopoiesis and lymphocyte development. Cytokines include interleukins, chemokines and other signalling molecules. Each cytokine acts through its own receptor on target cells, and these receptors include members of the immunoglobulin (Ig) superfamily and tumour necrosis factor (TNF).

data.name: Parasitology
data.description: Parasitology is the scientific discipline concerned with the study of parasites and parasitic diseases, including the distribution, biochemistry, physiology, molecular biology, ecology, evolution and clinical aspects of parasites, including the host response to these agents.

data.name: Brownian Motion
data.description: Brownian motion or pedesis (from Ancient Greek: πήδησις) is the random motion of particles suspended in a fluid (a liquid or a gas) resulting from their collision with the fast-moving molecules in the fluid. This pattern of motion typically alternates random fluctuations in a particle's position inside a fluid sub-domain with a relocation to another sub-domain. Each relocation is followed by more fluctuations within the new closed volume. This motion is named after the botanist Robert Brown, who was the most eminent microscopist of his time

synonyms: Collision with the fast-moving molecules in the fluid

data.name: Haematopoietic System
data.description: The haematopoietic system is the system of organs and tissues, including the bone marrow, spleen, thymus and lymph nodes, involved in the production of cellular blood components.

data.name: Categorization
data.description: Categorization in the field of psychology refers to the cognitive process of organizing information or stimuli into meaningful categories based on their shared features or characteristics. It involves grouping similar objects, events, or concepts together to simplify and make sense of the world.

data.name: Sociology of the Arts
data.description: Sociology of the Arts is a subfield of sociology that focuses on the analysis of the social dimensions of artistic production, consumption, and appreciation. This includes the study of the social organization of artistic institutions, the role of cultural capital in shaping artistic tastes and preferences, and the impact of art on societal values and identities.

data.name: Genetic Markers
data.description: Genetic markers are DNA sequences with known physical locations on chromosomes. They are points of variation that can be used to identify individuals or species, or may be used to associate an inherited disease with a gene through genetic linkage with nearby but possibly unidentified or uncharacterised genes. Examples include single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) and minisatellites.

data.name: Latin American Politics
data.description: Since the 1980s, presidential and general elections have been held in many countries in Latin America, and the election systems based on the multi-party system has taken root in these countries. At present, nearly all of the 33 Latin American and Caribbean countries have established democratic governments.

Latin America – Mexico, Central America, South America

data.name: e-Commerce and e-Business
data.description: The eCommerce and eBusiness industry refers to the use of electronic communication and information technologies to conduct business activities. It encompasses a wide range of activities, including online sales, marketing, payment processing, supply chain management, and customer service. As a field within business and management research and practice, eCommerce and eBusiness is concerned with understanding and optimizing the use of technology to improve business performance and create value for customers.  Core topics within eCommerce and eBusiness research and practice include:  Online consumer behavior and preferences, Digital marketing and advertising strategies, Web design and user experience optimization, Payment and security systems for online transactions, Supply chain and logistics management for eCommerce, Customer relationship management and customer service in an online environment, Legal and regulatory issues related to eCommerce, such as data privacy and intellectual property protection.

data.name: Model Protists
data.description: Model protists are extensively studied protists (unicellular and simple multicellular eukaryotes not categorized as animal, plant or fungus) chosen for the ease of investigating particular biological phenomena or for their relevance as disease agents.

data.name: Climate Change
data.description: Climate change refers to a statistically defined change in the average and/or variability of the climate system, this includes the atmosphere, the water cycle, the land surface, ice and the living components of Earth. The definition does not usually require the causes of change to be attributed, for example to human activity, but there are exceptions.

data.name: Mode-Locked Lasers
data.description: Mode-locked lasers generate short pulses of intense coherent light. Just like a guitar string, laser cavities can support many different frequencies, or resonant modes. A train of picosecond or femtosecond pulses can be produced by actively or passively controlling the light in the cavity so that these different resonant modes interfere.

data.name: Immunological Disorders
data.description: Immunological disorders are diseases or conditions caused by a dysfunction of the immune system and include allergy, asthma, autoimmune diseases, autoinflammatory syndromes and immunological deficiency syndromes.

data.name: Adipocytes
data.description: Adipocytes are cells specialised in storing energy as fat, mainly triglycerides, in organelles called lipid droplets. There are two major types of adipocytes in mammals: white adipocytes contain one large lipid droplet and are involved in fat storage, whereas brown adipocytes have many smaller lipid droplets and numerous mitochondria that generate energy, maintaining body temperature.

data.name: Dental Treatments
data.description: Dental treatment means dental care or dental services provided by dentists. It includes procedures such as cleaning teeth, filling cavities, extracting decayed tooth, crowning teeth, root canal therapy, etc.

data.name: Gastrointestinal Diseases
data.description: Gastrointestinal diseases are those that affect any section of the gastrointestinal tract, from the oesophagus to the rectum, and the accessory digestive organs, i.e. liver, gall bladder and pancreas. The term encompasses acute, chronic, recurrent or functional disorders and covers a wide range of diseases, including inflammatory bowel disease and functional dyspepsia.

subjects.term: Diseases of the stomach and duodenum

data.name: Clinical Signs and Symptoms
data.description: Signs and symptoms are abnormalities that can indicate a potential medical condition. Whereas a symptom is subjective, that is, apparent only to the patient (for example back pain or fatigue), a sign is any objective evidence of a disease that can be observed by others (for example a skin rash or lump).

data.name: Fluid Mechanics
data.description: Fluid mechanics refers to the mechanics of fluids (liquids, gases, and plasmas) and the forces on them. It has applications in a wide range of disciplines, including mechanical, chemical and biomedical engineering, geophysics, astrophysics, and biology. It can be divided into fluid statics, the study of fluids at rest; and fluid dynamics, the study of the effect of forces on fluid motion.

data.name: Virus
data.description: A virus is a microscopic infectious agent that replicates inside living cells of organisms. It consists of genetic material (either DNA or RNA) enclosed in a protein coat called a capsid. Viruses are considered obligate intracellular parasites because they require a host cell to replicate and complete their life cycle

data.name: Human Papilloma Virus
data.description: Human papilloma virus (HPV) is an infectious agent belonging to the virus family Papillomaviridae, members of which have tropism for cutaneous epithelium and mucosal epithelium. There are more than 120 different HPV types, with HPV-16 and HPV-18 having a strong association with cervical cancer.

data.name: Population Genetics
data.description: Population genetics is a subfield of genetics that deals with genetic differences within and between populations, and is a part of evolutionary biology. Studies in this branch of biology examine such phenomena as adaptation, speciation, and population structure. Traditionally a highly mathematical discipline, modern population genetics encompasses theoretical, lab, and field work. Population genetic models are used both for statistical inference from DNA sequence data and for proof/disproof of concept.Population genetics is the study of genetic variation within populations, and involves the examination and modelling of changes in the frequencies of genes and alleles in populations over space and time. (University of Leicester).Population genetics is the study of the genetic composition of populations, including distributions and changes in genotype and phenotype frequency in response to the processes of natural selection, genetic drift, mutation and gene flow.

data.name: Applications of Brownian Motion and Diffusion Theory
data.description: Applications of Brownian Motion and Diffusion Theory refer to the practical utilization of these concepts in various fields and disciplines. Brownian motion, which describes the random movement of particles suspended in a fluid, and diffusion theory, which provides a mathematical framework for understanding the spread and mixing of substances, have numerous practical applications.

synonyms: Practical Utilization of Brownian Motion and Diffusion Theory
Implementations of Brownian Motion and Diffusion Theory
Uses of Brownian Motion and Diffusion Theory

data.name: Data Processing
